lesson.title: The Information Molecules: An Introduction to Nucleic Acids
lesson.summary: Nucleic acids are polymers built from nucleotide monomers joined by condensation reactions, and the specific sequence of those monomers is what allows DNA and RNA to store and transmit genetic information.
lesson.body:
Nucleic acids form one of the major classes of biological macromolecule, alongside proteins, carbohydrates, and lipids, and like proteins they are polymers, long chains built from repeating monomer units. The monomers that make up nucleic acids are called nucleotides, and just as amino acids are joined end to end to build a protein, nucleotides are joined end to end to build a nucleic acid. This is the same general polymer building strategy used throughout biochemistry, and it depends on the same basic chemical reaction used to build proteins.

Nucleotides are linked together through condensation reactions, the same type of dehydration reaction that links amino acids into a polypeptide. In a nucleic acid, the phosphate group of one nucleotide reacts with the sugar of the next nucleotide, a water molecule is released, and a new covalent linkage called a phosphodiester bond is formed. Repeating this reaction many times over builds a long backbone of alternating sugar and phosphate units, with a sequence of nitrogenous bases hanging off to one side. As with proteins, this reaction runs in reverse through hydrolysis, where a water molecule is added back across a phosphodiester bond to break the chain apart, which is exactly how enzymes called nucleases break down nucleic acids, including the dietary nucleic acids we digest from the food we eat.

The phosphate group at the core of every phosphodiester bond is a strongly acidic functional group, and at the pH found inside cells it carries a negative charge. Because every nucleotide in the chain contributes one of these charged phosphates, the sugar phosphate backbone of a nucleic acid is negatively charged along its entire length. That negative charge has real consequences: it is part of why nucleic acids are so soluble in water, and it is the property that laboratory techniques like gel electrophoresis exploit to separate nucleic acid fragments by size.

Cells build two distinct types of nucleic acid. Deoxyribonucleic acid, or DNA, serves as the long-term, stable repository of genetic information, essentially the archived master copy of an organism's genetic instructions. Ribonucleic acid, or RNA, plays a more active role in reading and using that information, appearing in several forms with different jobs, including carrying genetic messages, delivering amino acids during protein synthesis, and forming the catalytic core of the ribosome itself. In certain viruses, RNA even serves as the primary genetic material in place of DNA.

In both DNA and RNA, it is the specific order of nucleotides along the chain that actually carries information, in much the same way that the specific order of amino acids along a polypeptide carries the instructions for how a protein will fold. A nucleic acid sequence and a protein sequence are both, at their core, linear strings of monomers whose exact order determines what the finished molecule can do, whether that is storing a gene or catalyzing a reaction.
